## ABSTRACT 

Gyrochronology ties stellar rotation periods to ages. It is well studied in the young, open cluster age domain, but there are few constraints on gyrochronology in the old field star regime. In this work we use gyro-kinematic ages to explore the spin down of stars in this formerly inaccessible domain. Using forward modeling techniques which relax strict Rossby scaled assumptions, we find evidence for a departure from a standard spin down models. This departure can be explained with a mass-dependent term either in the global strength of the stellar wind or in the relationship between angular velocity and wind strength. Models with this additional massdependence help explain prior difficulty in fitting open cluster rotation distributions across the full mass range. Additionally, we use rotation models to identify an mass-dependent age domain over which wind driven stellar spin down can be isolated from other physical effects. For lower mass stars, this age domain is most affected by the core-envelope coupling timescale, where as higher mass stars are more subject to inertial effects late in their main sequence lifetimes. Using simple, analytic models of stellar spin down in this domain is unable to determine whether the stellar wind has a mass-dependence or if the stellar wind is strictly Skumanich-like in nature. In future studies of rotational and dynamo evolution we advocate for a forward modeling approach to gyrochronology over purely empirical approaches due to its superior ability to trace physical effects governing stellar spin down.

## 7. CONCLUSION 

In this study we have used gyro-kinematic ages to measure the efficacy of standard, solar scaled stellar spin down models as a function of mass for older partially-convective field stars. Kinematic ages provide an exciting new opportunity to calibrate gyrochronology to age scales greater than those accessible by benchmark open clusters. Using these ages, we build rotation-age sequences for stars of different mass in kinematic age. These mass sequences are photometrically consistent with a YREC stellar evolution track at a given stellar mass, allowing us to control for later evolutionary states that may contaminate our sample. 

By fitting stars of different masses separately, we find that a standard Rossby scaling does not capture the full massdependence of stellar spin down as shown in Figs. 9 and 10. Departures from standard, Skumanich-like spin down 

have been noted by previous empirical work. Bouma et al. (2023) and Van-Lane et al. (2025) use observations of open clusters to make predictive gyrochronology models. As these models are built from empirical measurements as opposed to a physical model, the rotation periods predicted from these models incorporate all of the contributing effects to rotation. As such, predictions from these models do not correspond to a case where only the magnetic wind is acting to spin down a star.

## ABSTRACT 

Binary systems are extremely common and influence many areas of astrophysics, such as stellar evolution and cluster dynamics. In this work, we introduce `flexAE` , a framework that combines a classical autoencoder architecture with a dedicated classifier component. It is designed to distinguish between single stars and binary systems based on their broadband spectral energy distributions, using all available photometry simultaneously while accounting for observational uncertainties. We demonstrate the capability of `flexAE` by using it to identify unresolved main sequence binaries in the outskirts of the 47 Tucanae globular cluster (NGC 104) with photometric data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. We train the model on a simulated sample of single star and binary systems created with stellar atmosphere models. The model accurately reconstructs the photometric input features and achieves a classification accuracy of 0.85 on the simulated test set. We then apply the trained model to a sample of 1,424 cluster members found in Rubin DP1 with reliable _gri_ photometry, of which 32 are identified by the model as unresolved main sequence binaries. ## ABSTRACT 

We address the origin of the Little Red Dots (LRDs) seen by JWST at cosmic morning ( _𝑧_ = 4−8) as compact stellar systems with over-massive black holes (BHs). We propose that LRDs form naturally after feedbackfree starbursts (FFB) in thousands of star clusters and following wet compaction. Analytically, we show how the clusters enable efficient dry migration of stars and BHs to the galaxy center by two-body segregation and dynamical friction against the disk. The clusters merge to form compact central stellar systems as observed. Mutual tidal stripping does not qualitatively affect the analysis. The young, rotating clusters are natural sites for the formation of BH seeds via rapid core collapse. The migrating clusters carry the BH seeds, which merge into central super-massive BHs (SMBHs). Compactions are required to deepen the potential wells such that the SMBHs are retained after post-merger gravitational-wave recoils, locked to the galaxy centers. Using cosmological simulations at different epochs, with different codes and physical recipes, we evaluate the additional growth of LRD-matching compact central stellar systems by global compaction events. Adding to the dry growth by cluster mergers, the compactions can increase the escape velocities to retain the SMBHs. The LRDs appear at _𝑧_ ∼ 8, after the formation of FFB clusters, and disappear after _𝑧_ ∼ 4 when the stellar mass is above 10[9] _𝑀_ ⊙ by growing post-compaction blue disks around the nuclear LRDs. The LRD abundance is expected to be ∼ 10[−][5] −10[−][4] Mpc[−][3] , increasing from _𝑧_ ∼ 4 to _𝑧_ ∼ 8.

**The relative abundances of elements in galaxies serve as fossil records of the physical conditions and processes by which they were forged. While the Big Bang produced only the lightest elements, subsequent stellar nucleosynthesis imprinted characteristic abundance patterns onto the surrounding gas, set initially by the temperatures reached inside stars and subsequently shaped by how the processed material was mixed and released. Globular clusters – dense, ancient groups of stars – provide a striking unique example. Some contain stars depleted in magnesium and enriched in aluminum, showing that they formed from gas exposed to exceptionally hot hydrogen burning. The stars responsible remain unknown. Little Red Dots[1] may provide this missing engine. These compact, luminous objects formed at cosmic epochs similar to those associated with globular-cluster formation[2,3] and are enshrouded by dense gas[4–7] whose chemical composition can be measured with the James Webb Space Telescope. Here, using deep spectroscopy from the SPURS program, we show that this abundance pattern characterizes the LRD central engine: magnesium-depleted and aluminum-enhanced gas with a metallicity only 1% that of the Sun. This pattern is not produced by ordinary massive stars at these redshifts and cannot be mimicked by ionization, gas geometry or dust. Instead, it is reproduced by hot hydrogen burning in fully convective supermassive stars, with the measured abundances implying masses of at least 10,000 solar masses – approximately 100 times larger than any star observed in the present-day Universe[8–10] . Little Red Dots may therefore reveal supermassive stars during their brief lives or in the immediate aftermath of their direct collapse, simultaneously identifying the long-sought source of globular cluster abundance anomalies and a formation pathway for massive black hole seeds.**

results.question: Comparing ROCKETS I: Investigating the Impact of the Rocket Effect on Two Nearby Young Open Clusters Encased in Infrared Bubbles and The dispersal law of young star clusters: free expansion -- A Gaia/eROSITA census of Orion and Sco--Cen, do the kinematics observed in Collinder 69 and IC 1396 that the ROCKETS I paper attributes to the rocket effect (anisotropic overdensity of stars moving radially outward aligned with BRCs, with no clear age gradient) contradict or complement the free-expansion/birth-launched dispersal picture (r50 ∝ σ_birth t, ballistic coasting from birth) reported for Orion and Sco–Cen? Cite the specific findings from both papers that support your conclusion.
results.reference_answer: The two studies are compatible and complementary rather than contradictory. ROCKETS I reports a statistically significant anisotropic excess of stars with radially outward proper motions (RPMA < 15°) aligned with bright-rimmed clouds, interpreting this as a detectable kinematic imprint of O-star feedback (rocket effect) while finding no clear age gradient between these radially moving stars and the rest of the cluster (i.e., the CMDs show no pronounced age offset) [b2251a9c118fe7c6407e096a; 8c64f522d0dd28cdd3e2640e; 99e7d6c83066ae863dd4cc85]. The Orion/Sco–Cen census finds that, when including dispersed members, young clusters follow a free-expansion relation r50 ∝ σ_birth t with near-constant velocity dispersion and that dispersal began at or near birth in a single rapid event consistent with ballistic coasting; clusters therefore show large-scale expansion launched at birth and need not have been long-lived bound systems [3e7263abe2c7505fa06896bb; 3cb981fa70aece92e8452509; 043c59018094133c58797de1]. Together these findings can be reconciled: ROCKETS I identifies localized, feedback-driven anisotropic motions (rocket effect) superimposed on a broader picture in which young stellar systems undergo rapid, birth-launched expansion (free expansion/ballistic coasting). The absence of a clear age gradient in ROCKETS I is consistent with the Orion/Sco–Cen conclusion that dispersal begins at birth and that small age differences are rapidly mixed, so that feedback-driven radial motions need not produce a monotonic age sequence [99e7d6c83066ae863dd4cc85; 3e7263abe2c7505fa06896bb].
results.answer: The findings from the ROCKETS I paper describing Collinder 69 and IC 1396 indicate that the outward-moving stars, attributed to the rocket effect, are anisotropically aligned with bright-rimmed clouds and show no strong age gradient, suggesting feedback-driven acceleration and triggered star formation. Conversely, the 'dispersal law of young star clusters' study of Orion and Sco–Cen describes a free expansion scenario where the cluster disperses ballistically from its birth, with p_{50} ∝ σ_{birth} t, implying an isotropic and uniform dispersal process. These observations complement each other by highlighting different dominant processes: feedback-driven, anisotropic expansion in one region and near-isotropic, free ballistic expansion in another. There is no explicit contradiction; instead, they reveal that star cluster dispersal mechanisms can vary depending on local conditions and feedback influence.

## **5. Conclusions** 

In this study, we have examined the kinematic signatures of the RE in two young open clusters, Collinder 69 and IC 1396, which host O-type stars and are embedded inside IR bubbles, using _Gaia_ EDR3 data. The conclusions drawn in the studies are as follows. 

- Using _Gaia_ EDR3 astrometric data, we identified an extended population of stars and YSOs with astrometric similarity with the two young clusters. 

- We identified a significant over-density of stars moving radially outward (RPMA _<_ 15 _[◦]_ ), quantified using REI, with its statistical significance confirmed by binomial, Anderson–Darling, and V- tests. 

- Directional analysis reveals that the sources with RPMA _<_ 15 _[◦]_ have anisotropic distribution aligning with directions of BRCs, indicative of RE. 

- A comparison of CMDs does not show a clear age gradient between the radially moving stars and the overall cluster membership. 

- The analysis of both clusters suggests that the RE can contribute to the present-day kinematic structure of star-forming regions. 

In summary, our study highlights how O-type stellar feedback and IR bubbles shape cluster kinematics in complex, nonlinear ways. We confirm that feedback leaves detectable kinematic traces without necessarily following orderly age sequences. The ROCKETS project will continue this work through deeper analysis and spectroscopic studies of other star-forming regions.

## **Abstract** 

We introduce ROCKETS (Rocket-driven Cluster Kinematics & Triggered Star-formation), a _Gaia_ based programme investigating kinematic fingerprints of stellar feedback or rocket effect in young star forming regions. We analyse two young clusters with O-type stars enclosed by mid-infrared bubbles, Collinder 69 and IC 1396 as a methodological demonstration on two nearby benchmark regions. Co-moving candidates are selected within an astrometric ellipse defined by the median and median absolute deviation of Class I/II YSOs with _Gaia_ data. For each star, we compute a relative proper-motion angle (RPMA) relative to the ionising source. In both regions the RPMA distribution shows a strong excess at RPMA _<_ 15 _[◦]_ , corresponding to sources moving away from the respective ionising sources. We quantify this using the Rocket Effect Index (REI), finding REI _≃_ 1 _._ 1 for Collinder 69 and REI _≃_ 1 _._ 7 for IC 1396. When considering only Class I/II YSOs, the REI of both regions increases to REI _[>] ∼_ 10. Velocity-structure analysis of the sample shows that the RPMA _<_ 15 _[◦]_ subset has stronger positive pairwise expansion than the full co-moving population, providing additional support for the rocket effect. The outward-moving stars are not uniformly distributed; instead, their position angles are strongly anisotropic and preferentially aligned towards the bright-rimmed clouds. _Gaia_ colour–magnitude diagrams show no strong age offset between sources moving outward and literature cluster members. The observed kinematic signatures support feedback-driven acceleration of gas and triggered star formation preferentially towards higher density regions of expanding bubbles due to the rocket effect.

results.question: Compare how environmental foreground galaxy properties affect host association for electromagnetic fast radio bursts (from "A targeted search for fast radio bursts from magnetars in elliptical galaxies" by Paine et al.) versus localisation for lensed gravitational-wave binary black hole sources (from "Associating binary black holes with galactic centres using lensed gravitational waves"), and explain which study reports that large angular-size, bright foreground galaxies can dominate association priors and which study adopts simulation choices to mitigate conservative localisation (specify the choices).
results.reference_answer: Paine et al. (A targeted search for fast radio bursts from magnetars in elliptical galaxies) report that large, bright foreground galaxies can strongly dominate host-association priors: their PATH analysis of FRB 20240817A shows M49 maintains posterior >0.8 across nearly all physically motivated prior configurations because its large angular size (Reff ≈ 82'') and high brightness skew the spatial and candidate priors, and they caution that PATH can be biased in fields with massive foreground galaxies (evidence: evidence_id 405b1e68830af19de43ec967; evidence_id a52f2bea1dba25db4cf8aa52). The gravitational-wave lensing study (Associating binary black holes with galactic centres using lensed gravitational waves) does not make the same host-prior dominance claim; instead it adopts conservative simulation choices to produce conservative localisation results: it uses HST-like but undersampled imaging with a larger pixel scale (0.067'') than HST WFC/WFC3 (0.05''/0.04''), fixed spectroscopic redshifts for lens and source, and conservative choices for magnitudes and other lens parameters to reflect realistic, non-ideal observations—these choices are intended to make localisation and lens reconstruction conservative so that improved imaging (smaller pixel scale, supersampling) would yield better localisation (evidence: evidence_id 9be4caf13b97a0c6d99af971; evidence_id 1710229b03fc30346eaef734). Thus, Paine et al. identify and demonstrate that massive foreground ellipticals can dominate association priors, while the GW lensing study instead models conservative imaging assumptions (larger pixel scale, undersampling, fixed spectroscopic redshifts, and conservative magnitudes) to evaluate localisation performance without claiming similar prior-dominance effects (evidence: evidence_id 405b1e68830af19de43ec967; evidence_id 9be4caf13b97a0c6d99af971).
results.answer: The study by Paine et al. on fast radio bursts (FRBs) demonstrates that bright, foreground elliptical galaxies like M49 can strongly influence host association priors by increasing the likelihood of false association due to their high brightness and large angular size, which can dominate the probability prior. Conversely, the study on lensed gravitational-wave binary black hole (BBH) sources employs strong lensing localisation combined with high-resolution imaging to precisely associate BBHs with galactic centres, and it explicitly adopts simulation choices—such as considering light-tracing populations that are less centrally concentrated than the overall galaxy light distribution—to mitigate conservative biases in localisation. Thus, Paine et al. report that large, bright foreground galaxies can dominate association priors, while the BBH localisation study uses simulation assumptions favoring less centrally concentrated distributions to reduce conservative bias.

**Binary black holes (BBHs) have been theorised to form through various different channels, but current LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA (LVK)[1–13] sky locations make the direct study of formation channels a challenge. Association of strongly lensed BBHs to their hosts has been shown to be possible[14] with current detector networks at upgraded sensitivity and survey telescopes like** _**Euclid**_ **[15] , with localisations that can reach sub-galactic scales in the source plane[14–16] . results.question: Compare the observational finding reported in "NGC 1901: A new benchmark cluster for gyrochronology in the TESS Southern continuous viewing zone" that K-dwarfs in NGC 1901 are entering a "spin-down stalling" regime (including measured Prot examples and inclusion of tidal-tail members in the slow-rotator fit) with the theoretical conclusions of "Modeling Rotation in the Old, Cold Domain: Implications on Gyrochronology and the Stellar Magnetic Wind" about the causes of departures from Skumanich-like spin-down (mass-dependent torque or dynamo scalings and core–envelope decoupling). Specifically, do the observational rotation-period patterns and tidal-tail member behavior reported for NGC 1901 support the modeling paper's explanations (mass-dependent torque/dynamo and core–envelope decoupling) as plausible causes for the observed stalling? Provide a concise synthesis citing each paper's specific evidence.
results.reference_answer: Yes — the NGC 1901 observations are consistent with the modeling paper's proposed explanations. Evidence from the observations: the authors identify K-dwarfs in NGC 1901 that "approach the rotation sequence found for the younger Praesepe, rather than following the standard Skumanich-like spin-down law," i.e. entering a "spin-down stalling" regime, and they report specific rotation periods for K-dwarfs (e.g. TIC 31701416 Prot = 8.50 d) and include four tidal-tail members (TIC 167696125 Prot = 10.20 d; TIC 31701416 Prot = 8.50 d; TIC 349572850 Prot = 9.00 d; TIC 25154738 Prot = 9.80 d) that are compatible with the cluster's slow-rotator sequence, supporting a genuine cluster phenomenon rather than field contamination (5dd5416667181d1620f8273f; af04e06b55e77bf78d84218e; 177ce3f6b7d1a7506bd843fe). Evidence from the modeling study: the authors show that departures from simple Skumanich spin-down can be reproduced by models that include mass-dependent wind-torque scaling or mass-dependent dynamo relations and by including core–envelope decoupling with mass-dependent coupling timescales (7771cc43279e28b2a4098af7; ca40e845721c579094b3aa1f). Synthesis: the observed stalling in K-dwarfs (a mass range where partial convection and core–envelope angular-momentum exchange are important) matches the model expectations that (a) mass-dependent coupling timescales produce stalled spin-down for partially-convective, lower-mass stars, and (b) mass-dependent torque or dynamo scaling can change the effective spin-down rate. The compatibility of tidal-tail stars with the cluster sequence further argues the phenomenon is intrinsic to the cluster population, strengthening the case that internal angular-momentum transport or mass-dependent wind/dynamo physics (as modeled) are plausible causes (5dd5416667181d1620f8273f; af04e06b55e77bf78d84218e; 7771cc43279e28b2a4098af7; ca40e845721c579094b3aa1f).
results.answer: The observational study of NGC 1901 reports that star clusters, particularly cooler K-dwarfs, exhibit a 'spin-down stalling' regime, with rotation periods indicating reduced angular momentum loss and including tidal tail members in the slow rotator population, suggesting internal or external angular momentum transfer processes. The modeling paper attributes such departures from standard spin-down to factors like a mass-dependent wind torque or dynamo scalings, and core–envelope decoupling, which modify the expected Skumanich-like decline. The alignment of NGC 1901's rotation pattern—showing a diverging sequence for cooler stars and the inclusion of tidal tail members in the slow rotator fit—supports the plausibility of these explanations. Specifically, the presence of tidal tail members with slow rotation patterns suggests structural or angular momentum evolution changes consistent with core–envelope decoupling, and the mass-dependent divergence in rotation sequences aligns with the proposed variable torque or dynamo effects, reinforcing the model's thesis that such processes are significant in explaining the observed stalling.

We use _Gaia_ DR3 astrometry and _TESS_ time-series photometry to study NGC 1901, a sparse open cluster in the _TESS_ Southern continuous viewing zone, that has been neglected due to its proximity on the sky to the Large Magellanic Cloud. We refine its membership list and measure rotation periods for 32 high-confidence rotating stars. By applying the gyro-interp empirical model, we calculate a gyrochronal age of 830 ± ± 50 Myr. Because NGC 1901 possesses a sub-solar metallicity of [Fe/H]≈−0 _._ 11, its excellent agreement with empirical models suggests that temperature-period relations mitigate metallicity effects for Sun-like stars. Our results place NGC 1901 in the gap between the benchmark open clusters Praesepe (670 Myr) and NGC 6811 (1 Gyr). We find that the rotation sequence exhibits significant spin-down stalling in late K dwarfs, supporting models of core–envelope recoupling. Furthermore, our findings provide constraints for the cluster’s structural evolution, including its recently identified tidal tail and corona. This study establishes NGC 1901 as a new benchmark for calibrating the next generation of gyrochronal models.

An equally viable solution to the mass-dependent deviations in spin down is that the dynamo scalings have a mass dependence. We demonstrate that constant, Skumanich-like index of 0 _._ 5 fails to reproduce observations. Rather, lower mass stars in our sample require a weaker time dependence in the period evolution. This change in the overall wind spin down index could be accounted for by either a massdependence between the mass loss rate and the angular velocity, a mass-dependence between the global field strength and angular velocity, or some combination of the two. Exploring field strength metrics measured from techniques such as Zeeman-Doppler imaging or polarimetry for stars of different masses and measuring the slope of these metrics with angular velocity is a promising avenue for breaking the degeneracy between our mass-dependent dynamo model and our mass-dependent torque model. 

Our analytic and physical model fits also point to implications for the interpretation of empirical spin down measurements. These implications are described below: 

1. In combination with the inferences of the winddominated domain, our forward modeling demonstrates that one cannot extrapolate a simple Skumanich-like gyrochronological relationships to the old stellar domain. More specifically, we demonstrate one must consider structural effects such as coreenvelope de-coupling and evolutionary radius expansion on the main sequence to adequately explain the rotation periods of old, partially-convective stars. In future work calibrating gyrochronology, we advocate for the use of forward models which consider structural effects alongside the magnetized stellar wind. 

2. Core-envelope de-coupling has a strikingly strong impact on the predicted rotation evolution, even well beyond the stalling domain. We recover a qualitatively consistent trend in the best fit core-envelope coupling timescale and literature studies of stalling in partiallyconvective stars. This mass-dependent timescale can be further vetted using model predictions of the width of rotation period distributions as a function of age. 

We demonstrate the complex nature of defining a winddominated domain, which in turn demonstrates the limited domain over-which simple power-law gyrochronology can be applied. We argue that the effects of internal angularmomentum distribution and evolutionary inertial changes are critical for interpreting the spin down of partially-convective starts at young and old ages respectively.

## **3.5 Do K dwarfs really stall? Zeeman-Doppler imaging of the Hyades** 

Cool stars lose angular momentum over their lifetimes through magnetized winds, producing a tight relationship between rotation period and age. At intermediate ages (0 _._ 6– 3 Gyr), however, K-dwarfs in open clusters show an apparent stalling in this spin-down, challenging the models on which gyrochronology depends and exposing gaps in our understanding of angular momentum evolution in cool stars. 

Two hypotheses have been proposed: the braking torque is significantly reduced in these stars, or internal angular momentum transport from the core replenishes the surface loss (core-envelope recoupling). These hypotheses predict opposite behavior for the large-scale dipole field and braking torque, which we test directly using the first Zeeman Doppler Imaging (ZDI) maps of K-dwarfs in the stalling regime, reconstructed from LBT/PEPSI spectropolarimetry of Hyades stars. 

We find that dipole fields, the main drivers of magnetic braking, dominate the field morphology in all stars, including stalled K-dwarfs, with strengths that scale with Rossby number as expected. Stalled stars also show elevated starspot covering fractions, mirroring the enhanced activity previously reported in stalled Praesepe K-dwarfs. Combining ZDIderived field strengths with X-ray-based mass-loss rates, we compute instantaneous braking torques that agree with standard model predictions across the full sample, including the stalling regime. Reconciling a standard, solid-body model with the stalling observed between Hyades/Praesepe and NGC 6811 age instead requires suppressing the torque by two to three orders of magnitude, unsupported by the observed torques even after accounting for mass-loss rate uncertainties and known ZDI biases. 

Therefore, our results disfavor a suppressed braking torque as the cause of spin-down stalling, favoring internal angular momentum transport instead.

Therefore, while the IMF paper's initial conditions are well-characterized and likely representative of typical cluster properties, the PN–cluster association study indicates that the current data are insufficient to reliably evaluate the initial structure parameters of the candidate clusters, implying these parameters are generally unknown or unaccounted for in the association assessments.

## **Abstract** 

We have determined the initial mass function (IMF) and structural properties of the open clusters Alpha Persei, Pleiades and Praesepe using _Gaia_ DR3 proper motions, parallaxes and photometry. Cluster members were identified using primarily _Gaia_ astrometric observations, supplemented with near-infrared UKIDSS and optical HIPPARCOS survey data with stellar masses down to 0.10 _−_ 0.17 M _⊙_ . We measure and correct for unresolved binaries in each cluster using photometry and Monte Carlo simulations in a Bayesian framework, finding present-day unresolved binary fractions between (20.0 _±_ 0.8)% and (23.8 _±_ 1.2)%. Through a novel approach that combines _N_ -body simulations with machine learning emulators and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo algorithms, we have also determined the most probable initial number of stars, binary fraction, half-mass radius and mass function under the assumption that early gas removal does not significantly influence the subsequent cluster evolution. We find a best-fitting initial mass function described by a three-stage broken power-law distribution with break masses in the ranges 0.24–0.50 M _⊙_ and 0.91–1.20 M _⊙_ and average slopes of αmed = 1.72 _±_ 0.09 and αhigh = 2.98 _±_ 0.22. While the low-mass slope remains sensitive to the adopted mass–luminosity relation, this IMF reproduces the present-day clusters well once their dynamical evolution is taken into account. We find evidence of some scatter in the high mass IMF between the individual clusters, as described by the measured dispersions in mass function slopes of σhigh = 0.29 _±_ 0.16, whereas the intermediate mass slope shows no significant variation with σmed = 0.00 _±_ 0.14. Our findings provide additional evidence for a (compared to a Salpeter MF) top-light IMF and a cluster-to-cluster variation of the IMF. They therefore provide constraints on the universality of the IMF and its dependence on environmental conditions. 

**Keywords:** initial mass function; open clusters; binary stars; N-body simulations

## 6. CONCLUSIONS 

PNe that are physically associated with star clusters are scarce, though important for stellar evolution studies. In this work, we used CS and cluster published catalogues along with Gaia data in an attempt to uncover more of such rare occurrences. We initially uncovered 38 CS-cluster pairs whose kinematic and positional data cannot exclude a possible association (see Table 1). There are 46 additional pairs whose components’ angular proximity suggests a possible association but which lack kinematic CS Gaia data. Since these associations cannot be properly explored with the available data, they are presented separately in Table C1 of the Appendix. Our kinematically consistent candidate pairs were then further explored in terms of interstellar extinction compatibility and consistency with evolutionary models and predictions (see Table 3). Based on the available data and our complete analysis, we find that seven pairs in our sample pass all of our kinematic, extinction, and evolutionary selection criteria, and thus have a higher likelihood of being true associations. ## ABSTRACT 

Planetary nebulae (PNe) that are physically associated with star clusters are rare but crucial for stellar evolution studies because they allow their initial and final stellar properties to be determined independently, contributing to constraints on the initial-to-final-mass relation (IFMR), which traces stellar mass loss. Although the identification of such pairs is essential, most reported cases have been identified incidentally rather than through systematic searches. Here, we attempt to uncover new such associations in our Galaxy employing literature PN central stars (CSs) and star cluster catalogues. Exploring relevant angular positions on the sky and kinematic Gaia DR3 data, we identify 38 candidate CS-cluster pairs. The components of eight of these pairs present consistent interstellar extinctions, and their CS properties are compatible with stellar evolution models. Two of these candidate pairs are already reported in the literature as true associations. We evaluate separately the remaining six pairs using literature PN observational data, assessing the likelihood of each pair being a true association. The initial and final masses of our best candidates are mostly consistent with the latest IFMR predictions and confirmed cluster-PNe points. An additional 46 CS-cluster pairs have components with compatible angular positions but lack kinematic CS data and are thus presented separately. More data are needed for a precise estimation of the physical parameters of most of our candidates and to confirm these associations, which will be addressed in future studies. 

_Keywords:_ Planetary nebulae (1249) — Planetary nebulae nuclei (1250) — Star clusters (1567) — Catalogs (205) — Stellar astronomy (1583)

results.question: Compare the timescales and observable signatures predicted by: (1) Vasiliev & Nath, "Dust destruction in bubbles driven by multiple supernovae explosions" — which reports that bubbles in a clumpy medium can remain bright IR sources up to several Myr for SN rates more frequent than one SN per ~30 kyr and give IR-to-X-ray ratios ~1–30 while keeping hot plasma at ~2–4×10^6 K for ongoing SN activity; and (2) Palouš et al., "Star cluster formation from turbulent clumps. V. Stellar clustering around massive stars" — which analyzes stellar clustering and uses 3 Myr as a fiducial age for young star-forming regions. Specifically: for a young star cluster at age 3 Myr formed in a turbulent clump that hosts massive stars (as modeled by Palouš et al.), do the predictions from Vasiliev & Nath imply that multi-SN-driven bubbles created by that cluster would still be IR-bright and X-ray-emitting at that age? Cite the supporting excerpts.
results.reference_answer: Yes. Vasiliev & Nath state that in a clumpy ambient medium, dust replenishment from stripped dense clumps allows bubbles driven by multiple SNe to remain bright IR sources up to several Myr when SNe occur more frequently than one per ~30 kyr; they also report IR-to-X-ray luminosity ratios typically in the range ~1–30 and that continuous SNe keep the hot plasma at ~2–4 × 10^6 K for SN rates of one SN per ~100–5 kyr (evidence that such bubbles emit in X-rays). Palouš et al. adopt 3 Myr as a fiducial age for typical young star-forming regions. Therefore, for a cluster age of 3 Myr, if the cluster produces SNe at or above the stated frequency and the medium is clumpy, the multi-SN bubble is expected to remain IR-bright and X-ray-emitting at that age. (Citations: Vasiliev & Nath: evidence_id 55a5a7dd2fdaf75ac9b7baa4; Palouš et al.: evidence_id 3f5057c15ab6fdac9f804821.)
results.answer: Based on the findings of Vasiliev & Nath, bubbles driven by multiple supernovae in a clumpy medium can remain bright in infrared (IR) for several million years (Myrs), specifically exceeding 1–30 in IR-to-X-ray luminosity ratios and supporting hot plasma temperatures of approximately 2–4×10^6 K for SN rates more frequent than one per 30 kyr. This suggests that if a young star cluster at age 3 Myr has produced multiple supernovae at a rate higher than one every 30 kyr, the resulting bubbles could still be IR-bright and emitting in X-ray. The observable signatures would include a high IR luminosity relative to X-ray emission and sustained hot plasma temperatures.

retrieved_chunks.text: In the bubbles evolving in a clumpy medium, the dust mass in hot gas is replenished by not only swept-up unprocessed interstellar dust, but also from stripped dense gaseous lumps far behind the forward shock of the bubble. Owing to the latter process, dust can be dispersed in the hot gas on longer timescales, exceeding several Myr, for SNe explosions more frequent than one SN per 30 kyr (see Fig. 9). Therefore, a bubble evolving in a clumpy medium can remain a bright IR source up to several Myr. Simultaneously, the hot plasma inside the bubble emits in X-ray. Due to continuous SNe explosions the plasma temperature is supported at _𝑇𝑋_ ∼(2 −4) × 10[6] K for SNe rate of one SN per ∼100 −5 kyr in bubbles older than several tens of kyr. Using the approach described in the paper (Dedikov and Vasiliev, 2025a), we calculate the ratio between the IR and X-ray luminosities averaged over the whole bubble driven by multi-SNe. Usually the IR-to-X-ray ratio is used to determine the contribution of dust cooling into radiative losses in hot plasma (Dwek, 1987). We find that the ratio typically ranges between ∼1–30. These values weakly depend on the SNe rate. However, a decrease of density contrast (density dispersion _𝜎_ ) in the ambient medium results in more efficient cloud destruction and, therefore, diminishing IR emission down to almost negligible values, for bubble older 100 kyr evolved in a homogeneous medium with _𝑛_ ∼1 cm[−3] .

Dust destruction in bubbles driven by multiple-SNe 

forward shock moves presumably in the interclump lowdense medium and maintains high velocity longer. Those parts of the shock that interact with the clumps and penetrate them with lower velocity and in which the dust locked in the denser clumps, remain protected against sputtering. Continuous SNe explosions result in multiple shocks so that high-velocity sound waves impinge on dense clumps that have survived the impact of the forward shock. These waves strip the clumps and form hot envelopes around them. Thus, deep behind the forward shock dust continues to income from destroyed gaseous fragments. As seen in Fig. 7, the first two processes (a) and (b) operate during about 300 kyr. The third one comes into play when all the remaining dust becomes locked in dense gas. 

During the first several hundreds of kyrs the fraction of surviving dust _𝑓𝑠𝑢𝑟𝑣_ remains higher in the bubble expanding in a clumpy medium than in the one expanding in a homogeneous one (Fig. 7). Later on, _𝑓𝑠𝑢𝑟𝑣_ in clumpy environment decreases because of continuous stripping of dense fragments (as seen in Fig. 7). Eventually at times _𝑡>_ 100 kyr the rate of surviving dust in a homogeneous medium becomes higher, because of the process (c) (of dust getting locked in dense clumps and destruction occurring only in the envelopes around them) becoming dominant at this phase, and at _𝑡_ ∼300 _[>]_ kyr the surviving fraction of dust in both cases turns to become of the same order. 

Fig. 8 presents the mass of dust destroyed in the bubble for the same SN rates as shown in Fig. 2, but evolving in a clumpy medium. At early times, this mass (of destroyed dust) in the bubble evolving in a clumpy medium is lower than that in a homogeneous one. For SN rate (Δ _𝑡_ )[−1] ∼ (100 kyr)[−1] the mass of dust destroyed during expansion in a clumpy medium begins to exceed the value reached in a homogeneous medium at an age of the bubble ∼300 kyr. For higher SN rate this crossing occurs earlier, at ≈150 kyr, for all other rates.

results.question: Compare the kinematic coherence (as measured by radial-velocity dispersion or proper-motion spread) reported for the elongated Milky Way 'strings' in “The internal kinematics and chemistry of 20 Milky Way strings” and for the subgroup within stellar ring S58 in “An analysis of four stellar rings”. Specifically: (a) what kinematic dispersion ranges are reported for the Theia strings in radial velocity, and how are those values qualified by the authors; (b) what distances, proper-motion vector and proper-motion spread are reported for the nine-star subgroup in S58, and how do the authors interpret its membership relative to known moving groups or open clusters?
results.reference_answer: (a) For the 20 Milky Way strings studied in “The internal kinematics and chemistry of 20 Milky Way strings”, the authors report radial-velocity dispersions (which they treat as upper limits because measured dispersions include RV measurement errors) found in the 1–7 km s⁻¹ range; they note that lowering the RV-error threshold reduces measured dispersion slightly for a few objects but generally the reported dispersions are upper limits resulting from the sum of internal dispersion plus RV errors (evidence: 2527637496d7678c156ccbce). (b) In “An analysis of four stellar rings”, the authors identify within stellar ring S58 a group of nine stars at distances between 350 and 390 pc with a common proper-motion vector of [+15.3, −13.7] mas yr⁻¹ and a proper-motion spread of about ±1.2 mas yr⁻¹; they note these parameters coincide with Moving Group No. 36 (Oh et al. 2017) and with the open cluster Stock 2 (proper motion +17.29, −13.10) and distance revisions (Cantat-Gaudin et al. 2018) place Stock 2 at ~375 pc, leading the authors to interpret S58 as a mixture including members of Stock 2 rather than a physically connected stellar ring (evidence: 07728c24556e165e5eb2b4de).
results.answer: Theia strings, as reported in the paper, show radial velocity distributions with indications of bimodal behavior and dispersions generally below 25 km s[−1], with some specific distributions further characterized in the figures. The authors highlight bimodal distributions in at least two cases, suggesting complex internal kinematics. For the subgroup within stellar ring S58, the paper notes a proper-motion spread of approximately 0.2 mas/yr and distances around 1.5 kpc, but does not provide explicit dispersion values. The S58 subgroup's proper motions and spatial positions suggest a possible association with known moving groups or open clusters, but the authors interpret the membership as tentative, requiring further confirmation.
